danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 31
paragraphs: Da Pierre var redet ned ad bakken og havde fulgt generalen, drejede denne pludselig skarpt til venstre, og Pierre, der mistede ham af syne, galoperede ind mellem rækkerne af infanterister, der marcherede foran ham. Han forsøgte at komme forbi til højre eller venstre, men overalt var der soldater med samme forbavsede og irriterede udtryk i ansigterne, mens de udførte en eller anden usynlig, men tilsyneladende vigtig opgave. De kiggede alle med det samme utilfredse, spørgende blik på denne fyldige mand i hvid hat, der af ukendte grunde trampede løs på sin hest midt iblandt dem.
»Hvad laver den fyr midt i bataljonen!« råbte en af dem efter ham.
En anden stikker hans hest med kolben af en musket, og Pierre, der bøjede sig over sadelknappen og næsten ikke kunne styre sin sky hest, galoperede foran soldaterne derhen, hvor der var fri plads.

Foran ham lå en bro, hvor andre soldater stod og skød. Pierre red hen til dem. Uden selv at vide det var han kommet til broen over Kolotsja mellem Gorki og Borodino, den bro, franskmændene angreb i slagets første fase, efter at de havde indtaget Borodino. Pierre så, at der lå en bro foran ham, og at soldater havde noget for på begge sider af den og ude på engen mellem skårene af nyslået hø, som han dagen før slet ikke havde ænset i røgen fra lejrbålene. Men trods den uafbrudte skydning faldt det ham ikke ind, at dette var slagmarken. Han hørte ikke kuglerne, der peb fra alle sider, ænsede ikke projektilerne, der fløj hen over ham, så ikke fjenden på den anden bred. Længe bemærkede han heller ikke de døde og sårede, skønt mange faldt lige ved ham. Han så sig om med et smil, der blev ved at ligge om hans mund.
»Hvad laver den fyr foran linjen!« råbte nogen igen efter ham.
»Til venstre!... Hold til højre!« råbte mændene til ham.

Pierre drejede til højre og stødte uventet ind i en af Rajevskijs (general Rajevskij) adjudanter, som han kendte. Adjudanten kiggede argt på ham og ville åbenbart også have råbt noget, men genkendte ham og nikkede.
»Hvordan er du kommet herhen?« sagde han og galoperede videre.
Pierre, der følte sig malplaceret, intet havde at gøre og var bange for igen at komme i vejen for nogen, galoperede efter adjudanten.
»Hvad sker der her? Må jeg komme med?« spurgte han.
»Et øjeblik, vent lige!« svarede adjudanten, red hen til en svær oberst, der stod i engen, afleverede en besked og vendte sig derefter mod Pierre.
»Hvordan er du kommet herhen, greve?« spurgte han med et smil. »Stadig nysgerrig?«
»Ja, ja,« bekræftede Pierre.
Men adjudanten vendte sin hest og red videre.
»Herovre er det udholdeligt,« sagde han, »men ved Bagration (fyrst Bagration) på venstre fløj er det frygteligt hedt.«
»Virkelig?« sagde Pierre. »Hvor er det?«
»Kom med mig op på vores bakketop. Derfra kan vi overskue det, og i vores batteri er det stadig til at holde ud,« sagde adjudanten. »Vil du med?«
»Ja, jeg følger dig,« svarede Pierre og kiggede sig om efter sin staldknægt.

Først nu opdagede han de sårede, der vaklede af sted eller blev båret på bårer. På den samme eng, han havde redet over dagen før, lå en soldat med hovedet kastet underligt tilbage og huen faldet af, midt blandt de duftende rækker af tørret hø.
»Hvorfor har de ikke båret ham bort?« ville Pierre spørge, men da han så adjudantens strenge blik i samme retning, holdt han sig tilbage.
Pierre fandt ikke sin staldknægt og red med adjudanten ned gennem hulvejen til Rajevskijs redoute. Hans hest haltede efter adjudantens og rystede ham ved hvert skridt.
»Du er vist ikke vant til at ride, greve?« bemærkede adjudanten.
»Nej, det er ikke det, men hendes gangart virker så ujævn,« sagde Pierre forvirret.
»Jamen... hun er såret!« sagde adjudanten. »I det venstre forben over knæet. En kugle, utvivlsomt. Tillykke, greve — det er din ilddåb!«

Efter at have redet gennem røgen forbi Sjette Korps og bag artilleriet, der var rykket frem og var i fuld gang med at skyde, og som bedøvede dem med sine drøn, nåede de til en lille skov. Der var det køligt og stille, med en duft af efterår. Pierre og adjudanten steg af hestene og gik op ad bakken til fods.
»Er generalen her?« spurgte adjudanten, da de nåede bakketoppen.
»Han var her for et øjeblik siden, men er lige gået den vej,« sagde en, der pegede til højre.
Adjudanten så på Pierre, som om han var i tvivl om, hvad han skulle stille op med ham.
»Bryd dig ikke om mig,« sagde Pierre. »Jeg går op på bakketoppen, hvis det er i orden?«
»Gør det. Derfra kan du se alt, og det er mindre farligt. Jeg henter dig senere.«
Pierre gik hen mod batteriet, og adjudanten red videre. De mødtes aldrig igen, og først meget senere erfarede Pierre, at adjudanten havde mistet en arm den dag.

Bakketoppen, som Pierre besteg, var den berømte, der senere blev kendt af russerne som Bakke-batteriet eller Rajevskijs Redoute, og af franskmændene som la grande redoute, la fatale redoute, la redoute du centre — stedet, hvor titusinder faldt, og som franskmændene betragtede som hele stillingens nøglepunkt.
Denne redoute bestod af en bakketop med grave gravet på tre sider. Inden for forskansningen stod ti kanoner, der fyrede gennem åbninger i jordvolden.

I linje med bakken stod på begge sider andre kanoner, der ligeledes fyrede uafbrudt. Lidt bagved stod infanteri. Da Pierre besteg bakken, havde han ingen anelse om, at dette sted med de små grave og de få kanoner var det vigtigste punkt på hele slagmarken.
Tværtimod — netop fordi han tilfældigvis befandt sig dér, syntes han, det var et af de mindst betydningsfulde steder.

Pierre satte sig ned i den ene ende af en løbegrav, der omgav batteriet, og kiggede på, hvad der foregik omkring ham, med et ubevidst lykkeligt smil. Ind imellem rejste han sig og gik rundt i batteriet med det samme smil, idet han forsøgte ikke at komme i vejen for soldaterne, der ladede, trak og affyrede kanonerne. Disse soldater med deres muntre, venlige ansigter skiftede konstant glædesblik med ham, som om de allerede havde vænnet sig til hans tilstedeværelse.

I modsætning til den frygt, infanteristerne i reserven følte, herskede der her i batteriet — hvor et lille antal mænd var optaget af deres arbejde og adskilt fra resten af en grav — en fælles og nærmest familiær stemning af livlighed.

Indtrængen af Pierres umilitære skikkelse i hvid hat gjorde først et ubehageligt indtryk. Soldaterne kiggede forundret og endog uroligt på ham, da de passerede. Den ældre artilleriofficer, en lang, langbenet, koparret mand, kom hen til Pierre, som for at se kanonen virke, og kiggede nysgerrigt på ham.
En ung, rundkindet officer, næsten stadig en dreng og åbenbart lige ud af kadetskolen, der med stor iver kommanderede de to kanoner, han havde fået betroet, henvendte sig strengt til Pierre.
»Undskyld, min herre,« sagde han, »men De må stå til side. De kan ikke være her.«

Soldaterne rystede misbilligende på hovedet, da de kiggede på Pierre. Men da de havde overbevist sig om, at denne mand i den hvide hat ikke foretog sig noget skadeligt, men enten sad stille på skråningen af løbegraven med et genert smil eller høfligt gik til side for soldaterne og vandrede op og ned i batteriet under en hagl af kugler lige så roligt som på en boulevard — veg deres fjendtlige mistro lidt efter lidt for en godmodig, drillende hengivenhed af den slags, soldater nærer for deres hunde, haner og geder og alle de andre dyr, der lever med regimentet. Snart tog de Pierre ind i familien, adopterede ham, gav ham et kælenavn – »vores fine herre« – og morede sig hjerteligt over ham indbyrdes.
En granat rev jorden op to skridt fra Pierre, og han kiggede rundt med et smil, mens han børstede noget jord af, som den havde kastet op.
»Og hvordan kan det være, at De ikke er bange, min herre?« spurgte en rødmusset, bredskuldret soldat Pierre med et grin, der blottede et sæt hvide tænder.
»Er du bange?« sagde Pierre.
»Hvad tror du selv?« svarede soldaten. »Hun kender ingen nåde, hende dér! Når hun kommer hvislende ned, så er det ud med indvoldene. Man kan ikke lade være med at være bange,« sagde han med et grin.
Flere af mændene med lyse, venlige ansigter slog sig ned ved siden af Pierre. De havde tilsyneladende ikke ventet, at han talte som et almindeligt menneske, og opdagelsen glædede dem.
»Det er en sag for os soldater. Men at en herre gør det — dét er imponerende! Sikke en herre!«
»På plads!« råbte den unge officer til de mænd, der var stimlet sammen om Pierre.
Den unge officer udøvede tydeligvis sine pligter for første eller anden gang og behandlede derfor både sine overordnede og de menige med stor præcision og formalitet.

Kanonernes torden og musketildens knitren blev stadig voldsommere over hele slagmarken, især til venstre, hvor Bagrations flècher lå, men hvorfra Pierre var, gjorde røgen det næsten umuligt at skelne noget. Desuden var hele hans opmærksomhed opslugt af at iagttage den lille familiekreds af mænd, der var isoleret fra alt andet på batteriet. Hans første ubevidste glæde over synet og lyden af slagmarken var blevet afløst af en anden følelse — især efter synet af den enlige soldat, der lå på engen. Nu sad han på skråningen af graven og iagttog de ansigter, der omgav ham.

Ved titiden var en snes mænd allerede båret væk fra batteriet; to kanoner var ødelagt, og granater slog hyppigere og hyppigere ned i batteriet, og brugte kugler svirrede og fløjtede. Men mændene i batteriet syntes ikke at bemærke det; muntre stemmer og spøg hørtes fra alle sider.
»En levende!« råbte en mand, da en hvislende granat nærmede sig.
»Ikke herhen! Hen til infanteriet!« tilføjede en anden med høj latter, da granaten fløj forbi og slog ned blandt reserverne.
»Bukker du for en bekendt, hva'?« bemærkede en tredje og drillede en bonde, der dukkede sig, da en kanonkugle fløj henover.
Flere soldater havde samlet sig ved løbegravens mur og kiggede ud for at se, hvad der skete foran dem.
»De har trukket forlinjen tilbage — den er rykket bagud,« sagde de og pegede ud over jordvolden.
»Pas I bare jeres egne sager,« råbte en gammel sergent. »Hvis de er rykket tilbage, er det, fordi der er arbejde til dem længere bagude.«
Og sergenten greb en af mændene i skuldrene og gav ham et skub med knæet. Det blev fulgt af en latter.
»Femte kanon, rul den frem!« lød råb fra den ene side.
»Hejs ho, allesammen, som flodskippere!« lød de muntre stemmer fra dem, der rullede kanonen.

»Hovsa, den var lige ved at slå hatten af vores herre!« råbte den rødmussede humorist og viste tænder, mens han drillede Pierre. »Din tøs!« tilføjede han bebrejdende til en kanonkugle, der ramte et kanonhjul og en mands ben.
»Nå, I ræve!« sagde en anden og grinede ad nogle militsmænd, der bøjede sig ind i batteriet for at bære den sårede mand væk.
»Så den grød er vel ikke efter jeres smag? Kra, I krager! I er skræmt!« råbte de til militsmændene, der stod tøvende foran manden, der havde fået sit ben revet af.
»Nå nå, venner... åh, åh!« efterlignede de bønderne. »De bryder sig slet ikke om det!«
Pierre bemærkede, at efter hvert nedslag i redouten, og efter hvert tab, blev livligheden større og større.

Som flammerne fra en ild, der er skjult indeni, flammer stadig mere levende og hastigt op fra en truende tordensky, således, som i modstand mod det, der skete, voksede lynene af den skjulte ild stadig stærkere i disse mænds ansigter.

Pierre kiggede ikke ud over slagmarken og var ikke optaget af at vide, hvad der foregik dér; han var helt opslugt af at betragte denne ild, der brændte stadig klarere, og som han følte flammede op på samme måde i hans egen sjæl.

Klokken ti trak det infanteri, der havde stået i buskadset foran batteriet og langs Kamenka-bækken, sig tilbage. Fra batteriet kunne man se dem løbe tilbage forbi det med deres sårede på musketter. En general med sit følge kom til batteriet, og efter at have talt med obersten gik han igen, efter at have beordret infanteriet bag batteriet til at ligge ned for at mindske tabet fra ilden. Straks efter marsjerede infanteriet op fra højre side af batteriet, to og to; soldaterne kunne ses bære de sårede på musketter. Granater slog nu oftere ned i batteriet, og der var adskillige mand, der endnu ikke var bragt væk og lå og vred sig.
Pierre så over jordvoldens kant og blev særlig grebet af en bleg, ung officer, der gik baglæns med sværdet hængende ned langs siden og hele tiden kiggede uroligt omkring sig.

Infanteriets rækker forsvandt i røgen, men deres langtrukne råb og hurtige musketild kunne stadig høres. Få minutter senere kom skarer af sårede og bæremænd tilbage fra den retning. Projektiler slog stadig hyppigere ned i batteriet. Flere mænd lå uhjulpne. Soldaterne bevægede sig mere travlt og energisk omkring kanonerne. Ingen lagde længere mærke til Pierre. En gang eller to blev der argt råbt ad ham, fordi han var i vejen. Den ældre officer, med store, hurtige skridt, gik fra den ene kanon til den anden med et mørkt udtryk. Den unge officer, med endnu mere rødmen i kinderne, kommanderede sine mænd med endnu større iver. Soldaterne udleverede ladningerne, drejede, ladede og udførte deres opgaver med anspændt elegance. De hoppede i takt, som om drevet af fjedre.

Stormskyen havde nået dem, og i hvert eneste ansigt brændte den ild, Pierre havde set flamme op. Pierre stod ved den kommanderende officers side. Den unge officer, med hånden ved huen, løb hen til sin overordnede.
»Jeg har den ære at melde, hr. oberst, at vi kun har otte skud tilbage. Skal vi fortsætte ilden?« spurgte han.
»Kardæsker!« råbte den ældre, uden at besvare spørgsmålet, idet han kiggede over løbegravens mur.
Pludselig skete der noget: den unge officer gav et gisp og sank, bøjet dobbelt, ned på jorden som en fugl skudt i flugten. Alt blev mærkeligt, uklart og tåget for Pierres øjne.

En kanonkugle efter en anden hvislede forbi og ramte jordvolden, en soldat eller en kanon. Pierre, der før ikke havde lagt mærke til disse lyde, hørte nu intet andet. Til højre for batteriet løb soldater, der råbte »Hurra!«, ikke fremad, men bagud — syntes det Pierre.

En kanonkugle ramte den yderste kant af den jordvold, hvor han stod, og jorden smuldrede bort; en sort kugle blinkede for hans øjne og slog i samme sekund ned i noget. Nogle militsmænd, der var på vej ind i batteriet, løb den anden vej.
»Alle med kardæsker!« råbte officeren.
Sergenten løb hen til officeren og hviskede forskrækket (som en butler, der under middagen meddeler sin herre, at der ikke er mere af den vin, der er bedt om), at der ikke var flere ladninger.
»Slynglerne! Hvad laver de?« råbte officeren og vendte sig mod Pierre.
Officerens ansigt var rødt og forsvaret, og hans øjne glimtede under den rynkede pande.
»Løb til reserven og hent ammunitionskasserne!« skreg han vredt, idet han undveg Pierres blik og talte til sine mænd.
»Jeg går,« sagde Pierre.
Officeren svarede ikke, men skridtede hen til den modsatte side.
»Stands ilden... Vent!« råbte han.
Den mand, der var beordret af sted efter ammunition, stødte ind i Pierre.
»Herregud, min herre, det her er ikke noget sted for Dem,« sagde han og løb ned ad skråningen.
Pierre løb efter ham og undgik det sted, hvor den unge officer sad.

En kanonkugle, endnu en og en tredje fløj henover ham og slog ned foran, ved siden af og bag ham. Pierre løb ned ad skråningen. »Hvor er jeg på vej hen?« spurgte han sig pludselig, da han allerede var tæt på de grønne ammunitionsvogne. Han standsede ubeslutsomt, usikker på om han skulle vende om eller fortsætte. Pludselig kastede en voldsom kraft ham bagud til jorden. I samme øjeblik blændede et kæmpemæssigt glimtsyn ham, og et øredøvende brag, bragen og hvinen rungede i hans ører.

Da Pierre kom til sig selv, sad han på jorden og støttede sig på hænderne; de ammunitionsvogne, han havde været på vej hen til, var ikke mere — kun forkullede grønne brædder og klude strøet ud over det svedne græs. En hest, der slæbte stumper af sine stænger efter sig, galoperede forbi, mens en anden lå dødsstille og jamrede sig, og Pierre kiggede på den og forstod ikke, hvad der foregik.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 31
paragraphs: Having descended the hill, the general Pierre was chasing turned sharply to the left, and Pierre, losing sight of him, galloped into ranks of infantry marching ahead. He tried to pass them on the right or the left, but soldiers were everywhere, all with the same preoccupied expressions, busy with some unseen but clearly important task. They all stared with dissatisfied, questioning looks at this heavyset man in a white hat who, for some unknown reason, threatened to trample them under his horse's hooves.
"Why are you riding into the middle of the battalion?" one of them shouted at him.
Another poked his horse with the butt of a musket, and Pierre, leaning over his saddlebow and barely able to control his shying horse, galloped ahead of the soldiers to an open space.

There was a bridge ahead, where other soldiers stood firing. Pierre rode up to them. Without realizing it, he had reached the bridge across the Kolocha between Gorki and Borodino, which the French — having occupied Borodino — were attacking in the first phase of the battle. Pierre saw that there was a bridge in front of him and that soldiers were doing something on both sides of it and in the meadow, among the rows of freshly mown hay he hadn't noticed through the campfire smoke the day before; but despite the incessant firing, he had no idea this was the actual battlefield. He didn't notice the bullets whistling from every side or the projectiles flying over him, didn't see the enemy on the other side of the river, and for a long time didn't notice the killed and wounded, though many fell near him. He looked about him with a smile that never left his face.
"Why is that fellow in front of the line?" somebody shouted at him again.
"To the left! Keep to the right!" men shouted at him.
Pierre went to the right and unexpectedly ran into one of Raevsky's adjutants, whom he knew. The adjutant looked angrily at him, clearly about to shout, but recognizing Pierre he simply nodded.
"How did you get here?" he said, and galloped on.
Pierre, feeling out of place, with nothing to do, and afraid of getting in someone's way again, galloped after the adjutant.
"What's happening here? May I come with you?" he asked.
"One moment, one moment!" the adjutant replied, and riding up to a stout colonel standing in the meadow, delivered some message, then turned to Pierre.
"Why have you come here, Count?" he asked with a smile. "Still curious?"
"Yes, yes," Pierre agreed.
But the adjutant turned his horse and rode on.
"It's tolerable here," he said, "but on the left flank with Bagration, they're taking a frightful pounding."
"Really?" said Pierre. "Where is that?"
"Come along with me to our knoll. We can get a view from there, and at our battery it's still bearable," said the adjutant. "Will you come?"
"Yes, I'll come with you," Pierre replied, looking around for his groom.

It was only now that he noticed wounded men staggering along or being carried on stretchers. In the very meadow he had ridden across the day before, a soldier lay sprawled across the rows of sweet-smelling hay, his head thrown awkwardly back, his cap fallen off.
"Why haven't they carried him away?" Pierre was about to ask, but seeing the grim expression on the adjutant's face as he too looked that way, Pierre held his tongue.
Pierre couldn't find his groom and rode along the hollow with the adjutant toward Raevsky's Redoubt. His horse lagged behind the adjutant's and jolted him at every step.
"You don't seem very used to riding, Count," the adjutant remarked.
"No, it's not that — her gait just seems so jerky," Pierre said in a puzzled tone.
"She's been wounded!" said the adjutant. "In the left foreleg above the knee. A bullet, no doubt. Congratulations, Count — your baptism of fire!"

Having ridden through smoke past the Sixth Corps, behind the artillery that had been moved forward and was firing — deafening them with its roar — they came to a small wood. There it was cool and quiet, with the smell of autumn. Pierre and the adjutant dismounted and walked up the hill on foot.
"Is the general here?" the adjutant asked on reaching the knoll.
"He was here a minute ago but just went that way," someone told him, pointing to the right.
The adjutant looked at Pierre, as if unsure what to do with him now.
"Don't worry about me," said Pierre. "I'll go up onto the knoll if I may."
"Yes, do. You'll see everything from there and it's less dangerous. I'll come for you."
Pierre went to the battery and the adjutant rode on. They never met again, and only much later did Pierre learn that the adjutant had lost an arm that day.

The knoll Pierre climbed was the famous one later known to the Russians as the Knoll Battery or Raevsky's Redoubt, and to the French as the great redoubt, the fatal redoubt, the redoubt of the center — around which tens of thousands fell, and which the French considered the key to the entire position.
This redoubt consisted of a knoll with trenches dug on three sides. Within the earthworks stood ten guns being fired through openings in the walls.

On both sides of the knoll stood other guns, also firing without pause. A little behind the guns stood infantry. Climbing the knoll, Pierre had no idea that this spot — with its small trenches and handful of guns firing away — was the most critical point of the entire battle.
On the contrary, just because he happened to be there, he thought it one of the least significant parts of the field.

Having reached the knoll, Pierre sat down at one end of the trench surrounding the battery and watched what was happening around him with an unconsciously happy smile. Now and then he stood up and walked about the battery, still smiling, trying not to get in the way of the soldiers who were loading, hauling guns, and constantly running past him with bags and charges. The guns were firing continuously, one after another, with a deafening roar that enveloped the entire area in powder smoke.

In contrast to the dread felt by the infantrymen positioned in support behind them, here in the battery — where a small group of men busy at their work were separated from everyone else by a trench — there was a shared, almost family-like feeling of excitement.

Pierre's unmilitary figure in a white hat made an unfavorable impression at first. The soldiers looked at him sideways with surprise and even alarm as they passed. The senior artillery officer, a tall, long-legged, pockmarked man, moved over to Pierre as if to check the aim of the farthest gun, and studied him with curiosity.
A young round-faced officer, practically a boy, clearly fresh out of the Cadet College and zealously commanding the two guns assigned to him, addressed Pierre sternly.
"Sir," he said, "please step aside. You must not be here."

The soldiers shook their heads disapprovingly at Pierre. But when they had satisfied themselves that this man in the white hat was doing no harm — either sitting quietly on the trench slope with a shy smile, or politely stepping aside for the soldiers as he strolled up and down the battery under fire as calmly as if walking on a boulevard — their hostile distrust gradually turned into a warm, teasing affection, like the kind soldiers feel for their dogs, roosters, goats, and other animals that live with the regiment. They quickly adopted Pierre into their family, gave him a nickname — "our gentleman" — and made fond fun of him among themselves.
A shell tore up the earth two paces from Pierre, and he looked around with a smile as he brushed the dirt it had thrown up from his clothes.
"How is it you're not afraid, sir — really?" a red-faced, broad-shouldered soldier asked Pierre with a grin that showed a set of strong white teeth.
"Are you afraid, then?" said Pierre.
"What do you expect?" the soldier answered. "She's got no mercy! When she comes sputtering down — out go your guts. You can't help being scared," he said, laughing.
Several men with bright, friendly faces stopped beside Pierre. They seemed not to have expected him to talk like a normal person, and the discovery that he did delighted them.
"It's our job as soldiers. But for a gentleman — that's something! There's a real gentleman for you!"
"Back to your posts!" the young officer called to the men gathered around Pierre.
The young officer was clearly performing his duties for the first or second time and therefore treated both his superiors and the men with great precision and formality.

The booming cannonade and rattle of musket fire were growing more intense across the whole field, especially to the left where Bagration's fortifications were, but where Pierre stood the smoke made it nearly impossible to see anything. Besides, his entire attention was absorbed in watching the tight-knit family circle — sealed off from everything else — formed by the men in the battery. His first unconscious surge of joyful excitement from the sights and sounds of the battlefield had now been replaced by a different feeling, especially since he'd seen that soldier lying alone in the hayfield. Now, sitting on the trench slope, he studied the faces around him.

By ten o'clock about twenty men had already been carried away from the battery; two guns were smashed, and cannonballs landed more and more frequently, while spent bullets buzzed and whistled around. But the men in the battery seemed not to notice any of this — cheerful voices and jokes could be heard on all sides.
"A live one!" shouted a man as a whistling shell approached.
"Not this way! Go to the infantry!" added another with loud laughter, watching the shell fly past and fall into the supporting ranks.
"Bowing to a friend, are you?" remarked another, teasing a militiaman who ducked low as a cannonball flew over.
Several soldiers gathered by the trench wall, peering out to see what was happening in front.
"They've pulled back the front line — it's retreated," they said, pointing over the earthwork.
"Mind your own business," an old sergeant shouted at them. "If they've fallen back, it's because there's work for them farther behind."
And the sergeant, grabbing one of the men by the shoulders, shoved him with his knee. This was followed by a burst of laughter.
"To the fifth gun — wheel it up!" came shouts from one side.
"All together now, like bargemen!" came the cheerful voices of the men moving the gun.

"She nearly knocked our gentleman's hat off!" cried the red-faced joker, showing his teeth and teasing Pierre. "Clumsy thing!" he added reproachfully to a cannonball that struck a cannon wheel and a man's leg.
"Come on, you foxes!" said another, laughing at some militiamen who, stooping low, entered the battery to carry away the wounded man.
"Don't like this porridge, do you? Scared crows!" they shouted at the militiamen who stood hesitating before the man whose leg had been torn off.
"Come on, lads... oh, oh!" they mimicked the peasants. "They really don't like it!"
Pierre noticed that after every hit on the redoubt, and after every loss, the liveliness only grew.

Like the flames of a hidden fire leaping more and more vividly from an approaching thundercloud, so — as if in defiance of what was happening — the lightning of an inner fire glowed ever more intensely in the faces of these men.

Pierre didn't look out at the battlefield and didn't care what was happening there; he was entirely absorbed in watching this fire that burned ever more brightly, and he felt it flaming up in the same way in his own soul.

At ten o'clock the infantry that had been in the bushes in front of the battery and along the Kamenka stream retreated. From the battery they could be seen running back past it, carrying their wounded on their muskets. A general and his staff came to the battery, spoke to the colonel, gave Pierre an angry look, and then left, ordering the infantry supports behind the battery to lie flat so as to be less exposed to fire. After this, from among the infantry ranks to the right of the battery came the sound of a drum and shouts of command, and from the battery they could see those infantry ranks moving forward.
Pierre looked over the trench wall and was particularly struck by a pale young officer who, his sword hanging down, was walking backward, glancing around anxiously.

The infantry ranks disappeared into the smoke, but their drawn-out shout and rapid musket fire could still be heard. A few minutes later, crowds of wounded men and stretcher-bearers came back from that direction. Shells began to fall even more frequently on the battery. Several men lay about, not yet removed. Around the cannon, the men moved still more briskly. No one paid attention to Pierre anymore. Once or twice he was shouted at for being in the way. The senior officer strode with big, rapid steps from gun to gun, his face set in a deep frown. The young officer, his face even more flushed, commanded his men with ever greater intensity. The soldiers passed up charges, turned, loaded, and performed their tasks with strained precision. They moved with little springy steps, as though walking on springs.

The storm had come upon them, and in every face the fire Pierre had watched kindle now blazed brightly. Pierre stood beside the commanding officer. The young officer, his hand to his cap, ran up to his superior.
"I have the honor to report, sir, that only eight rounds are left. Should we continue firing?" he asked.
"Grapeshot!" the senior officer shouted, without answering the question, looking over the trench wall.
Suddenly something happened: the young officer gasped and, folding double, sat down on the ground like a bird shot on the wing. Everything became strange, confused, and hazy in Pierre's eyes.

One cannonball after another whistled by, striking the earthwork, a soldier, or a gun. Pierre, who hadn't noticed these sounds before, now heard nothing else. To the right of the battery, soldiers were running and shouting "Hurrah!" — but backward, it seemed to Pierre.

A cannonball struck the very end of the earthwork where he was standing, crumbling the earth; a black ball flashed before his eyes and at the same instant plunged into something. Some militiamen entering the battery ran back.
"All grapeshot!" the officer shouted.
The sergeant ran up to the officer and informed him in a frightened whisper — like a butler telling his master that they've run out of a requested wine at dinner — that there were no more charges.
"The scoundrels! What are they doing?" the officer shouted, turning toward Pierre.
The officer's face was red and sweating, his eyes glittering under his furrowed brow.
"Run to the reserves and bring up the ammunition boxes!" he yelled, angrily avoiding Pierre with his eyes and speaking to his men.
"I'll go," said Pierre.
The officer, without answering, strode to the opposite side.
"Don't fire! Wait!" he shouted.
The man who had been ordered to go for ammunition stumbled against Pierre.
"This is no place for you, sir," he said, and ran down the slope.
Pierre ran after him, avoiding the spot where the young officer sat.

One cannonball, another, and a third flew over him, falling in front, beside, and behind him. Pierre ran down the slope. "Where am I going?" he suddenly asked himself when he was already near the green ammunition wagons. He halted in confusion, not knowing whether to return or go on. Suddenly a terrible blast threw him backward to the ground. At the same instant he was blinded by a great flash of flame, and immediately a deafening roar, a crackling and whistling made his ears ring.

When he came to his senses he was sitting on the ground, leaning on his hands; the ammunition wagons he'd been approaching no longer existed — only charred green boards and rags littered the scorched grass. A horse, trailing fragments of its shaft, galloped past, while another lay on the ground like Pierre, uttering long, piercing cries.
